claim: Tuning of individual neurons is coarse, with visual receptive field diameters that can exceed perceptual resolution.
source: Because tuning of individual neurons is coarse (e.g., visual receptive field diameters can exceed perceptual resolution), the populations of neurons potentially responsive to each individual stimulus can overlap, raising the question of how information about each item might be segregated and preserved in the population.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on receptive field properties.

claim: Some neurons in macaque visual cortical areas V1 and V4 exhibited fluctuating firing patterns when two stimuli were present, as if they responded to only one individual stimulus at a time.
source: We recently reported evidence for a potential solution to this problem: when two stimuli were present, some neurons in the macaque visual cortical areas V1 and V4 exhibited fluctuating firing patterns, as if they responded to only one individual stimulus at a time (Jun et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Fluctuating activity is evoked by multiple stimuli in the middle temporal visual area (MT).
source: Here, we provide new evidence that such fluctuating activity is also evoked by multiple stimuli in visual areas responsible for processing visual motion (middle temporal visual area, MT), and faces (middle fundus and anterolateral face patches in inferotemporal cortex – areas MF and AL), thus extending the scope of circumstances in which fluctuating activity is observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fluctuating activity is evoked by multiple stimuli in the middle fundus (MF) face patch in inferotemporal cortex.
source: Here, we provide new evidence that such fluctuating activity is also evoked by multiple stimuli in visual areas responsible for processing visual motion (middle temporal visual area, MT), and faces (middle fundus and anterolateral face patches in inferotemporal cortex – areas MF and AL), thus extending the scope of circumstances in which fluctuating activity is observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fluctuating activity is evoked by multiple stimuli in the anterolateral (AL) face patch in inferotemporal cortex.
source: Here, we provide new evidence that such fluctuating activity is also evoked by multiple stimuli in visual areas responsible for processing visual motion (middle temporal visual area, MT), and faces (middle fundus and anterolateral face patches in inferotemporal cortex – areas MF and AL), thus extending the scope of circumstances in which fluctuating activity is observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MT exhibits fluctuations between the representations of two stimuli when these form distinguishable objects but not when they fuse into one perceived object.
source: Furthermore, consistent with our previous results in the early visual area V1, MT exhibits fluctuations between the representations of two stimuli when these form distinguishable objects but not when they fuse into one perceived object, suggesting that fluctuating activity patterns may underlie visual object formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and comparison to previous findings.

claim: Fluctuating activity patterns may underlie visual object formation.
source: Furthermore, consistent with our previous results in the early visual area V1, MT exhibits fluctuations between the representations of two stimuli when these form distinguishable objects but not when they fuse into one perceived object, suggesting that fluctuating activity patterns may underlie visual object formation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Neurons in primary visual cortex typically have receptive fields that are several times larger than spatial acuity at the perceptual level.
source: For example, even in primary visual cortex, neurons typically have receptive fields that are several times larger than spatial acuity at the perceptual level (Dow et al., 1981; Smith et al., 2001; Motter, 2009; Freeman and Simoncelli, 2011; Grill-Spector et al., 2017; Keliris et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: When two stimuli co-occur, individual neurons may fluctuate between responding to only one or the other stimulus at a time.
source: We recently reported a potential solution to this problem: When two stimuli co-occur, individual neurons may fluctuate between responding to only one or the other stimulus at a time, allowing dynamic populations of neurons to encode different stimuli at the same time.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' previous work and data presented in this manuscript.

claim: Fluctuating activity patterns allow dynamic populations of neurons to encode different stimuli at the same time.
source: We recently reported a potential solution to this problem: When two stimuli co-occur, individual neurons may fluctuate between responding to only one or the other stimulus at a time, allowing dynamic populations of neurons to encode different stimuli at the same time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the observed fluctuating activity.

claim: Evidence for fluctuating activity was found in the inferior colliculus when two distinguishable stimuli were presented.
source: In particular, we found evidence for fluctuating activity in the inferior colliculus (Caruso et al., 2018), primary visual cortex (V1), area V4 (Jun et al., 2022), and the middle fundus (MF) face patch of inferotemporal (IT) cortex (Caruso et al., 2018) when two distinguishable stimuli were presented.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Evidence for fluctuating activity was found in primary visual cortex (V1) when two distinguishable stimuli were presented.
source: In particular, we found evidence for fluctuating activity in the inferior colliculus (Caruso et al., 2018), primary visual cortex (V1), area V4 (Jun et al., 2022), and the middle fundus (MF) face patch of inferotemporal (IT) cortex (Caruso et al., 2018) when two distinguishable stimuli were presented.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Evidence for fluctuating activity was found in area V4 when two distinguishable stimuli were presented.
source: In particular, we found evidence for fluctuating activity in the inferior colliculus (Caruso et al., 2018), primary visual cortex (V1), area V4 (Jun et al., 2022), and the middle fundus (MF) face patch of inferotemporal (IT) cortex (Caruso et al., 2018) when two distinguishable stimuli were presented.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Evidence for fluctuating activity was found in the middle fundus (MF) face patch of inferotemporal cortex when two distinguishable stimuli were presented.
source: In particular, we found evidence for fluctuating activity in the inferior colliculus (Caruso et al., 2018), primary visual cortex (V1), area V4 (Jun et al., 2022), and the middle fundus (MF) face patch of inferotemporal (IT) cortex (Caruso et al., 2018) when two distinguishable stimuli were presented.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Oscillatory patterns of activity triggered by the appearance of multiple stimuli have been observed in V4 using other paradigms and analysis methods.
source: Relatedly, oscillatory patterns of activity triggered by the appearance of multiple stimuli have also been observed in V4 using other paradigms and analysis methods (Kienitz et al., 2018; Kienitz et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Activity fluctuation has been identified in a wide array of brain areas, from early auditory regions to early, middle, and late visual cortical regions.
source: In short, activity fluctuation has now been identified in a wide array of brain areas, from early auditory regions to early, middle, and late visual cortical regions.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from the authors' previous work and the current manuscript.

claim: Fluctuating activity may reflect a general mechanism of neural representation supporting the encoding of multiple stimuli.
source: This breadth of brain areas suggests that fluctuating activity may reflect a general mechanism of neural representation supporting the encoding of multiple stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the breadth of findings across brain areas.

claim: Neuronal activity in MT, MF, and AL fluctuated across trials between responses that appeared to be drawn from the response distributions corresponding to the respective individual stimuli.
source: We report that neuronal activity in all three areas fluctuated across trials between responses that appeared to be drawn from the response distributions corresponding to the respective individual stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In MF and AL, fluctuating neuronal activity was present when two faces were presented as well as when a face and a non-face object were presented.
source: In MF and AL, fluctuating neuronal activity was present when two faces were presented (i.e., stimuli for which the patches are specialized) as well as when a face and a non-face object were presented, but in MF the fluctuations were more common when two faces were presented (i.e., two stimuli of the category for which the neurons appear specialized) than when a face and a non-face object (different stimulus categories) were presented.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In MF, fluctuations were more common when two faces were presented than when a face and a non-face object were presented.
source: In MF and AL, fluctuating neuronal activity was present when two faces were presented (i.e., stimuli for which the patches are specialized) as well as when a face and a non-face object were presented, but in MF the fluctuations were more common when two faces were presented (i.e., two stimuli of the category for which the neurons appear specialized) than when a face and a non-face object (different stimulus categories) were presented.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Multiple faces compete more severely for representation in the face-specific system than do non-face objects.
source: This suggests that multiple faces compete more severely for representation in this face-specific system than do non-face objects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed difference in fluctuation prevalence between face-face and face-object pairs.

claim: In MT, fluctuating activity was present only when the two visual stimuli were distinct (adjacent gratings or dot patches), and not when they were superimposed and fused to form single objects (plaids).
source: In MT, such fluctuating activity was present only when the two visual stimuli were distinct (adjacent gratings or dot patches), and not when they were superimposed and fused to form single objects (plaids), thus implicating fluctuating activity as playing a role in perceptual segregation of distinct visual elements into distinct objects, supporting previous findings in V1 (Jun et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fluctuating activity plays a role in perceptual segregation of distinct visual elements into distinct objects.
source: In MT, such fluctuating activity was present only when the two visual stimuli were distinct (adjacent gratings or dot patches), and not when they were superimposed and fused to form single objects (plaids), thus implicating fluctuating activity as playing a role in perceptual segregation of distinct visual elements into distinct objects, supporting previous findings in V1 (Jun et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed pattern of fluctuating activity in relation to stimulus distinguishability.

claim: Fluctuating activity patterns are a widespread phenomenon connected to the computations underlying object formation and identification.
source: Together, these findings suggest that fluctuating activity patterns are a widespread phenomenon connected to the computations underlying object formation and identification.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings across multiple brain areas and stimulus conditions.

claim: Object separation appears generally necessary for fluctuating activity to occur.
source: Object separation appears generally necessary for fluctuating activity to occur, and specialization for certain types of stimuli can also affect the prevalence of fluctuations across the neural population.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed differences between distinct and fused stimuli.

claim: Specialization for certain types of stimuli can affect the prevalence of fluctuations across the neural population.
source: Object separation appears generally necessary for fluctuating activity to occur, and specialization for certain types of stimuli can also affect the prevalence of fluctuations across the neural population.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed differences between face-face and face-object pairs in MF.

source: The first dataset included single- and multi-unit responses to drifting grating stimuli positioned adjacent to one another (Figure 1a.1 and 2; Ruff and Cohen, 2016b).

source: In both of these MT datasets, the stimuli can be considered as distinct and distinguishable objects from each other, regardless of whether they are gratings or patches of moving dots, because they are presented at separate locations.

claim: The MT plaid dataset involved simultaneous V1 and V4 recordings previously analyzed for fluctuating activity in Jun et al., 2022.
source: This dataset was originally published in Ruff et al., 2016a and involved simultaneous V1 and V4 recordings previously analyzed for fluctuating activity in Jun et al., 2022.

source: For the IT cortex, we included datasets involving single-unit recordings in two areas of the face patch system, areas MF and AL, during a fixation task (Figure 1c; fixation maintained within 1 degree) (Ebihara, 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the datasets with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Fixation was maintained within 1 degree in the IT datasets.
source: For the IT cortex, we included datasets involving single-unit recordings in two areas of the face patch system, areas MF and AL, during a fixation task (Figure 1c; fixation maintained within 1 degree) (Ebihara, 2015).

claim: Fluctuating activity was previously reported in face patch MF.
source: We have previously reported fluctuating activity in face patch MF (Caruso et al., 2018), but here we have re-analyzed the MF dataset (see 'Analysis: response periods and inclusion criteria') to provide detailed results for different types of stimuli (face–face vs. face–object pairs), allowing a comparison of results in the two face patches (MF and AL) in the same experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: For both MF and AL, neural responses were assessed to image pairs drawn from three visual stimuli: a 'preferred face', a 'non-preferred face', and a 'non-preferred object'.
source: For both MF and AL, we assessed neural responses to image pairs drawn from three visual stimuli selected from a pool of faces and objects: a 'preferred face' (strong neural response), a 'non-preferred face' (little to no neural response), and a 'non-preferred object' (little to no neural response).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus selection procedure.

claim: The preferred face evoked a strong neural response.
source: For both MF and AL, we assessed neural responses to image pairs drawn from three visual stimuli selected from a pool of faces and objects: a 'preferred face' (strong neural response), a 'non-preferred face' (little to no neural response), and a 'non-preferred object' (little to no neural response).
evidence: This is a description of stimulus selection criteria.

claim: The non-preferred face evoked little to no neural response.
source: For both MF and AL, we assessed neural responses to image pairs drawn from three visual stimuli selected from a pool of faces and objects: a 'preferred face' (strong neural response), a 'non-preferred face' (little to no neural response), and a 'non-preferred object' (little to no neural response).
evidence: This is a description of stimulus selection criteria.

claim: The non-preferred object evoked little to no neural response.
source: For both MF and AL, we assessed neural responses to image pairs drawn from three visual stimuli selected from a pool of faces and objects: a 'preferred face' (strong neural response), a 'non-preferred face' (little to no neural response), and a 'non-preferred object' (little to no neural response).
evidence: This is a description of stimulus selection criteria.

claim: Stimuli were randomly presented either alone or in pairs, with each pair including the preferred face positioned at the center of the neuron's receptive field and one of the non-preferred stimuli presented adjacent to the preferred face at one of eight equidistant locations.
source: These stimuli were randomly presented either alone or in pairs, with each pair including the preferred face, positioned at the center of the neuron's receptive field, and one of the non-preferred stimuli, presented adjacent to the preferred face at one of eight equidistant locations.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus presentation procedure.

claim: Stimuli in the IT datasets were 4 × 4 degrees in size.
source: Stimuli were 4 × 4 degrees in size.

claim: The exact location of the non-preferred face/object was not incorporated into the present analysis.
source: As in Caruso et al., 2018, we did not incorporate the exact location of the non-preferred face/object into the present analysis, but any excessive heterogeneity in the responses of the non-preferred stimuli due to location would likely result in exclusion of the condition from further analysis (see 'Analysis: response periods and inclusion criteria').
evidence: This is a description of the analysis approach with citation.

claim: For each dataset, neural responses were compared using a spike counting window of 200 ms.
source: For each dataset, we compared neural responses (see 'Data analysis') using a spike counting window of 200 ms, the minimum stimulus presentation window across all datasets.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: 200 ms was the minimum stimulus presentation window across all datasets.
source: For each dataset, we compared neural responses (see 'Data analysis') using a spike counting window of 200 ms, the minimum stimulus presentation window across all datasets.
evidence: This is a description of experimental parameters.

claim: The spike counting window was shifted by the approximate response latency of the brain region, specifically 30 ms for MT and 50 ms for IT.
source: This window was shifted by the approximate response latency of the brain region, specifically 30 ms for MT and 50 ms for IT, that is, spikes were counted in a window from 30 to 230 ms after stimulus onset for MT or 50–250 ms for IT.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method accounting for neural response latencies.

claim: For the IT datasets, the stimuli were presented for 400 ms.
source: For the IT datasets, the stimuli were presented for 400 ms, and results were similar when we analyzed the data in a 50–450 ms time window.

claim: Results for the IT datasets were similar when data were analyzed in a 50–450 ms time window.
source: For the IT datasets, the stimuli were presented for 400 ms, and results were similar when we analyzed the data in a 50–450 ms time window.
evidence: This is a description of robustness of the findings to different analysis windows.

claim: Only correctly performed trials were analyzed.
source: Only correctly performed trials were analyzed.

claim: For fixation tasks, correctly performed trials meant that the monkey maintained fixation for the required interval.
source: For fixation tasks, this meant that the monkey maintained fixation for the required interval (MT plaid dataset, IT datasets).
evidence: This is a description of behavioral performance criteria.

claim: For attention tasks, correctly performed trials meant that the monkey correctly identified the change in the attended stimulus.
source: For attention tasks, this meant that the monkey correctly identified the change in the attended stimulus, which was outside the receptive field of the neurons under study (MT gratings dataset: the motion change in a grating presented in the ipsilateral field; MT dot patch dataset: the change in color in the fixation target).
evidence: This is a description of behavioral performance criteria.

claim: Trials were excluded from the MT gratings dataset if any microsaccades were identified during the stimulus presentation period.
source: In addition, trials were excluded from the MT gratings dataset if any microsaccades were identified during the stimulus presentation period.
evidence: This is a description of trial exclusion criteria.

claim: Microsaccades were defined as periods of time in which eye speed exceeded the mean eye speed in the fixation epoch by more than 6 standard deviations.
source: Microsaccades were defined as periods of time in which eye speed exceeded the mean eye speed in the fixation epoch by more than 6 standard deviations, following standards established by Engbert and Kliegl, 2003 and deployed in our previous studies involving these same experiments (Ruff et al., 2016a; Ruff and Cohen, 2016b; Jun et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a description of the microsaccade detection method with citations.

claim: The analysis of fluctuating activity patterns relies on comparing the activity evoked on trials in which two stimuli, A and B, are presented simultaneously (AB) to trials in which only the A or only the B stimulus was presented.
source: Our analysis of fluctuating activity patterns relies on comparing the activity evoked on trials in which two stimuli, A and B, are presented simultaneously (AB) to trials in which only the A or only the B stimulus was presented.

source: First, the minimum number of included trials for each of the A, B, and AB components was set at five trials for each, in keeping with our prior work and assessments of the sensitivity of the analysis to the number of trials involved (Caruso et al., 2018; Mohl et al., 2020; Jun et al., 2022).

claim: The MT 'plaid' dataset had the most trials (average ~37 trials).

evidence: This is a description of dataset characteristics.

claim: Spike count distributions for the A- and B-alone trials in a triplet were required to be sufficiently well described by a Poisson distribution.
source: Second, spike count distributions for the A- and B-alone trials in a triplet were required to be sufficiently well described by a Poisson distribution (with a variance roughly equal to the mean).

claim: The previous chi-square goodness of fit approach had the undesired effect of being more likely to exclude conditions with larger amounts of data.
source: The former approach had the undesired effect of being more likely to exclude conditions with larger amounts of data, whereas the present method is neutral to dataset size.

claim: The present variance-to-mean ratio method is neutral to dataset size.
source: The former approach had the undesired effect of being more likely to exclude conditions with larger amounts of data, whereas the present method is neutral to dataset size.
